Security model

How SATOM protects sign-in, sessions, stored credentials and the host it runs on — accounts and privileges, permissions, CSRF and headers, encryption at rest and in transit, and the audit trail.

👤 ForAdministratorAdvanced user
📍 WhereServer side; related settings under Settings (Authentication, Vault, Node TLS) and Users / Profiles

Overview#

SATOM holds administrator credentials for every appliance it manages, so its security model has two goals: nobody gets more than their profile allows, and a compromise of the web process does not turn into root on the host or into a readable copy of every appliance password.

Layer Control
Host Unprivileged service account; root only in one on-demand runner
Network TLS at nginx; gunicorn and the metrics store bound to loopback
Sign-in Rate limits, per-account lockout, optional TOTP, optional directory sources
Authorisation Granular permissions in profiles, checked on every route
Browser CSRF tokens, strict Content-Security-Policy, no-store on HTML
Data at rest Fernet encryption of stored secrets; optional external vault
Inter-node HTTPS-only peer requests to a verified certificate, each HMAC-signed with the node identity key (the key never crosses the wire); TLS-enforced PostgreSQL replication
Accountability Audit log with the real client IP

Accounts and privileges#

The service account#

On installs made with installers/install-satom.sh, the application runs as an unprivileged account, satom by default (override with SATOM_APP_USER). It owns /opt/satom and /var/log/satom. The .env file is root:satom, mode 0640: the application can read its secrets but cannot rewrite them.

Unit Runs as
satom.service (web) service account
satom-scheduler.service, satom-reconciler.service service account
satom-alerts.service, satom-cert-renew.service service account
satom-integrations.service, satom-responder.service, satom-metrics.service service account
satom-ha-datasync.service (cluster installs) service account
satom-updater.service root — the only privileged unit

❗Important — Why User= lives in a drop-in

Some unit templates in deploy/ still declare User=root (web, scheduler, reconciler), and every software update copies them again. The installer therefore pins the account in a systemd drop-in (/etc/systemd/system/<unit>.d/10-app-user.conf) for every SATOM service except satom-updater.service, taking the list from the shipped unit templates; the self-update runner rewrites the same drop-ins on every update. Do not edit User= in the unit files by hand. (Before 2.11.0 the installer's list missed the integration hook runner, so with a custom SATOM_APP_USER hooks did not run until the first update.)

sudo#

The runtime sudoers file /etc/sudoers.d/satom allows the service account exactly two commands, used when a new TLS certificate is activated:

Cmnd_Alias SATOM_CERT_RELOAD = /usr/sbin/nginx -t, /usr/bin/systemctl reload nginx

If the host's sudo policy does not honour that file, certificate activation falls back to the privileged runner. Package installation and unrestricted systemctl are deliberately not granted: permission to install a package is permission to run any code as root.

A separate, temporary rule (/etc/sudoers.d/satom-installer, printed by install-satom.sh --print-sudoers) lets a named installer account run only the installer script from a root-owned path. Remove it when the installation window closes.

The privileged runner#

  1. 1Web workerwrites a JSON request into data/update-requests/
  2. 2satom-updater.pathnotices the directory is not empty
  3. 3satom-updater.service (root)re-validates the request against its own allow-list
  4. 4Actionpip upgrade, unit install, service restart, promotion…
  5. 5Resultstatus written to data/update-status/<id>.json, health check, roll back on failure

The web process cannot pass a command, only a request; the runner's own validation is the security boundary. The runner itself is installed as a root-owned copy outside the application tree (deploy/install-runner.sh), so the service account cannot rewrite the code root executes. The runner validates the request id, the git branch and target, rejects any request kind it does not recognise, and writes its status files without following symbolic links.

Signed releases (root-side content)#

The runner installs root-side content from deploy/ — the unit files, the install-*.sh scripts, the operator CLI and the runner copies — and the service account can edit deploy/. Signed-release enforcement pins that content to a release an operator signed. It is activated per node by installing a trust anchor; with no anchor, enforcement is off and updates behave exactly as before.

  • Anchor: /etc/satom/release-trust.allowed_signers (root:root, mode 0644), one line per trusted key: satom-release namespaces="git" ssh-ed25519 AAAA…. A single key at /etc/satom/release-trust.pub also works. Install it on both nodes of a high-availability pair.
  • Verification runs in a root-only mirror (/var/lib/satom-release/), never inside /opt/satom, so nothing the service account writes into the repository's git configuration or attributes is ever executed by root.

With an anchor, every update falls into one of three cases:

Case Root-side content comes from Update result
The target commit is signed the target normal
The target is unsigned, but deploy/ is identical to its newest signed ancestor that signed ancestor (the same bytes) normal
deploy/ changed since the last signed release nothing new: the root-side refresh is held the application still updates; the update shows the warning step root-side refresh held

An unsigned change to deploy/ therefore never blocks an update, so the standby keeps converging with the primary; only the root-side refresh waits for a signature.

Signing a release — on the primary, as root:

  1. sudo satom execute sign-release — a dry run: it shows the deploy/ diff since the last signed release.
  2. sudo satom execute sign-release --yes — adds one signed, empty commit on top of main with the root-only key /root/.satom-release/release_ed25519 and pushes it. The key never becomes readable by the service account.
  3. satom get release trust (with sudo for the full view) — shows the anchor, the newest signed commit and whether HEAD's deploy/ matches it.

The satom execute reinstall verbs (cli, runner, metrics-store, units) follow the same rule: with an anchor they install from a root-only staged copy of the signed release, and while deploy/ has unsigned changes they refuse and name satom execute sign-release as the fix.

Rollback: remove the anchor file(s) on both nodes; the next update runs with enforcement off.

ℹ️Note

Changed on 2026-10-14: enforcement became activatable without blocking high availability. The first version refused an update whose deploy/ was unsigned; now the application updates and only the root-side refresh is held. Root also no longer runs git inside the service account's repository, and the single-key .pub anchor works.

The separate integration-hook runner runs untrusted hook code as the unprivileged service account inside a tight sandbox: besides the read-only system and the single writable queue directory, it masks the on-disk secrets (/opt/satom/.env, the internal-CA key under pki/, the HA key under .ssh/) and hides other processes, so a hook cannot read the Fernet key or the database URL from disk.

The operator CLI#

The satom command is a root tool for a human operator. It is installed as a root:root copy under /usr/local/lib/satom-cli/, never run from /opt/satom, and must never be granted to the service account through sudo.

Running as root, the CLI never executes the application tree: the venv's Python, flask, pip and git against /opt/satom run as the service account (git would otherwise run programs named in the repository's own configuration as root). The venv is rebuilt as that account, files staged under data/ are written after dropping privileges, and permission repairs never follow a symbolic link or touch a hard-linked file. See CLI.

Sign-in protection#

Control Value
Sign-in rate limit 5 POSTs per minute per client IP
2FA challenge rate limit 10 per minute
Password recovery 5 per 15 minutes (request), 10 per 15 minutes (reset link)
Per-account lockout 10 consecutive failures → account locked for 15 minutes. Wrong 2FA codes count too (audited as login.2fa_fail)
2FA challenge lifetime 5 minutes after the password is accepted; after that the sign-in starts over
Local password length 12 to 1024 characters, length only (no character-class rule), on every path: web forms (Profile → Change Password, Add User, administrator reset, reset link), the CLI and both installers. Existing passwords are not re-validated
Idle session lock Settings → General → Session Lock (minutes) (5–1440, default 60): a browser session idle for longer is signed out on its next request
Local password hashing scrypt
Second factor TOTP for local accounts, with one-time backup codes

When locked, the sign-in page shows "Too many failed attempts — account temporarily locked. Try again later." A successful sign-in resets the failure counter; with 2FA on, only the accepted code does (the password alone does not). After signing in, SATOM returns you only to a page of the console itself: a next address that names another site, or hides one behind a tab or backslash, is replaced by the home page.

  • Local accounts never fall through to a directory. If a local user exists, only its local password is checked, so a directory account with the same name cannot take it over.
  • Directory sources (Active Directory, LDAP, RADIUS) are tried in the order set under Settings → Authentication; the first that accepts the credential wins. Users created on first directory sign-in get the global default profile and may need administrator approval first. See Users and profiles.
  • TOTP secrets are stored Fernet-encrypted; backup codes only as salted SHA-256 hashes. Password-reset links are signed, expiring tokens.
  • The reset link cannot be pointed elsewhere. The shipped nginx vhost forwards the request's Host header verbatim, and the Forgot password form is unauthenticated. The mailed link therefore keeps the request's host only when it is the node's own host name or FQDN, or is listed in LINK_HOSTS (see Configuration files); any other host is replaced by the node FQDN. Requests are still answered for every Host, so by-IP health and peer probes are unaffected.
  • Rate limits key on the real client IP. X-Forwarded-For is honoured only when the direct peer is listed in TRUSTED_PROXIES (default 127.0.0.1,::1), and the last hop is used so a client cannot forge it.

ℹ️Note — Rate-limit storage

With the default RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI=memory://, each gunicorn worker keeps its own counters. Point it at a local Redis (redis://…) so all workers share one set of limits.

Permissions#

Pages and actions require sign-in (@login_required; the /healthz probes and the sign-in pages are the exceptions) and a permission check (require_permission(...)), which returns 403 when the user's profile lacks the key. Every page that shows device content needs a read permission too:

Pages Key
Audit Log audit.view
Appliance pages appliances.view
FortiWeb workspace, protection, exceptions, artifacts, server objects, object editor, wizard, fleet objects protection.view
Monitoring pages, attack search, FortiADC / FortiAnalyzer / FortiAuthenticator pages, transaction tracer, certificate inspector the coarse view key
API-Registry Explorer and product API consoles registry.view
Sentinel monitoring.view
DNS tool network.view

The Global home lists appliances only to holders of appliances.view. The sidebar asks the same check as the page: a link is shown only when the user can open that page. The token API has its own scope checks — see API.

ℹ️Note

Changed in 2.11.0: pages that show device content need a read permission instead of sign-in alone (a custom profile with no read keys now gets 403 there), the sidebar hides links the user cannot open, failed local sign-ins are audited as login.fail, every password path enforces one 12-character minimum, and Session Lock is enforced as an idle timeout.

  • Granular keys (area.action, for example appliances.apply) are what profiles store and what you assign. The full list is on the Permissions page.
  • Five legacy coarse keys are still checked by many routes: view, backup, config_write, registry_edit, user_manage. A user holds a coarse key when their profile holds any of the granular keys that map to it:
Coarse key Granted by any of
view the *.view keys and monitoring.probe_free
backup backups.create, backups.restore
config_write protection / network edit and apply, operations.apply, the template keys, appliances.edit, appliances.apply
registry_edit registry.edit
user_manage users.manage
  • Seeded system profiles: readonly (all view keys), operator (view keys plus backups, protection, network, operations, templates, appliances and advisor.use), admin (every key).
  • Holders of user_manage are exempt from the IP allow-list, so a typo in the allow-list cannot lock out the administrators who must fix it.

Browser and session protection#

Headers#

Every response carries:

Header Value
X-Frame-Options DENY (plugin sandbox frames set SAMEORIGIN; their CSP allows images from data: only, so plugin code cannot send data out)
X-Content-Type-Options nosniff
Referrer-Policy strict-origin-when-cross-origin
Content-Security-Policy default-src 'self'; scripts and <style> elements only from self or with the nonce; script-src-attr 'none' (inline on…= handlers cannot run)
Cache-Control on HTML no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, max-age=0

Every response also carries Strict-Transport-Security (max-age of one year, scoped to the node's own host — no includeSubDomains/preload, so other services under the same parent domain are unaffected); browsers ignore it over plain HTTP, so it is harmless on a local run. No third-party origin is allowed: every script, stylesheet and font is served from the node itself, so SATOM works on isolated management networks.

The CSP nonce is generated once per session, not per request, because Turbo Drive page swaps keep the original document (and the nonce its header enforces).

Because script-src-attr 'none' blocks inline handlers, confirmation dialogs (for example before deleting a process, a change type or an artifact version) are attached by the shared script through a data-fw-confirm-form attribute, never through an onsubmit= attribute that the browser would silently ignore.

Session cookie#

SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE, SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY and SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE=Lax are set. Because the cookie is Secure, a browser never returns it over plain HTTP: if the TLS terminator is bypassed, no password can be accepted and SATOM says so explicitly ("This SATOM is served over plain HTTP while its session cookies are marked Secure…").

Idle lock. Every page load, Turbo visit and form submission records the user's last activity; timer-driven background polls (notification bell, job dock, edit-lock heartbeat, status badges) do not. A request that arrives more than the configured Session Lock (minutes) after the last activity signs the user out and shows "Your session was locked after N minutes of inactivity." (script callers get HTTP 401). Requests to the token API (/api/v1) have no session and are not affected; an Authorization header on any other request does not exempt it.

Remember me sets a separate cookie that is Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax and lasts 14 days.

Unauthenticated health probes#

/healthz answers every caller, but without a valid node signature it returns only ok and peer_authenticated. The revision, host statistics and database state, and the /healthz/backups, /healthz/cert-renewals and /healthz/reconciler probes (403 for an unsigned caller), are for the peer node, which signs every request (see In transit). /healthz/primary keeps its status code for load balancers and never returns database error text.

CSRF and the reverse proxy#

All state-changing requests need a CSRF token (Flask-WTF CSRFProtect, token lifetime 3600 s). JavaScript reads the token from a meta tag and sends it with every fetch. When a token is missing or stale, SATOM does not show a raw 400: the browser is sent back to the form with "Your session expired or the form was stale — please try again."; JSON callers get {"ok": false, "error": "CSRF token missing or expired — reload the page and retry"} with HTTP 400.

⚠️Warning — Behind a non-standard port, pass Host with the port

Over HTTPS, Flask-WTF also compares the browser's Referer — which includes the port — with the host the application sees. nginx's $host drops the port, so with proxy_set_header Host $host; behind a NAT or a proxy on a port other than 443 every POST, sign-in included, is rejected with the "session expired" message. Always use:

proxy_set_header Host $http_host;

The installer-generated vhost already does this. satom diagnose nginx flags a proxied vhost that uses $host, and satom execute repair nginx --yes rewrites it.

Credentials at rest#

Secret Stored as
Appliance passwords, directory bind passwords, RADIUS/FortiAuthenticator secrets, TOTP secrets, node identity key Fernet-encrypted with FERNET_KEY
User passwords scrypt hash
API tokens one-way hash of the secret; shown once at creation
2FA backup codes salted SHA-256 hashes

FERNET_KEY and SECRET_KEY live in /opt/satom/.env. FERNET_KEY is the one secret that cannot be regenerated: losing or changing it makes every stored credential undecryptable. In production SATOM refuses to start without it rather than generating a temporary key per worker.

⚠️Warning — The two secrets no backup carries

System backup bundles deliberately exclude FERNET_KEY and the internal CA key (pki/internal-ca/ca.key). A bundle restored onto a rebuilt node without them is a database of unreadable secrets. Keep them safe with satom execute export recovery-key or seal them with a passphrase using satom execute seal recovery (the envelope is written to data/recovery/seal.json and travels with backups and the HA sync). See System backup.

External vault (optional)#

Settings → Vault adds a second place for credentials (a Vault KV v2 store, AppRole or token authentication). Modes:

Mode Label Effect
local (default) Store in SATOM only (Fernet) The vault is never contacted.
mirror Store in both — read vault first, fall back to SATOM Migration mode; the local copy still exists.
vault Store in the vault only The local column holds a marker; a vault outage makes credentials unavailable.

Only the vault authentication token is cached; secret values are read through every time so the vault's own audit log stays accurate. The vault address — like the Sentinel model endpoint — must be an http(s) URL: any other scheme is refused before a request is made, so neither setting can be used to read the node's own files through a file:// address.

Local data protection#

The service runs with UMask=0022 on purpose (nginx must read the ACME webroot), so the protection lies in the directory modes. Nothing under /opt/satom/data/ is served by nginx, and no other local account (web server, mail server, Redis, a monitoring agent) can read it:

Path Mode
data/ 0750, owned by the service account, whose group has no other members
data/backups/ (device configuration vault), data/system_backups/ (system bundles), data/acme/, data/recovery/, data/pki-shared/ directories 0700, files 0600
  • System bundles are written through a private file descriptor, 0600 from the first byte, never narrowed after the archive is complete; a bundle fetched back from the off-box backup server is written the same way. Vault entries are written 0600 in 0700 directories, and a vault directory an older release left open is narrowed on its next write.
  • satom diagnose data (also part of satom diagnose all) reports any entry looser than this; sudo satom execute repair data --yes narrows them. The update runner runs the same repair after every update, and the installer sets data/, the vault and the bundle store to these modes on a fresh install and narrows them on a reinstall. See CLI and Data and storage.

In transit#

  • Browser ↔ node: TLS at nginx (TLS 1.2 / 1.3). Every install provisions a certificate; manage it under Node TLS.
  • Node ↔ appliance: HTTPS to the appliance API. Verification uses the Trust store; SSH channels pin host keys — an unreadable pin store is treated as a broken control and the connection is refused.
  • Node ↔ node: peer requests (health probes, peer settings and metrics collection) are HTTPS-only on :8443; there is no plain-HTTP fallback.
  • Request signing. Every peer request carries X-SATOM-Node-Ts and X-SATOM-Node-Sig: an HMAC-SHA256 over the method, path and query, the timestamp and a hash of the body, keyed with the shared node identity key. The key itself never crosses the wire. The receiver recomputes the signature and refuses one whose timestamp is more than 120 seconds from its own clock, so a captured request can be neither altered nor replayed later. The legacy static header X-FM-Node-Key is no longer accepted. Keep both nodes' clocks NTP-synchronised: a skew beyond 120 s makes every peer view read not authenticated.
  • Certificate verification. The peer's certificate must verify against the system trust store or the internal CA (host-name matching is off because peers are addressed by IP). An untrusted certificate is refused, with the reason logged, instead of silently downgrading. The emergency override SATOM_PEER_TLS_ALLOW_UNVERIFIED=1 in .env restores an encrypted-but-unverified retry; it is off by default and meant to be temporary — install a trusted node certificate under Node TLS instead.
  • /healthz reports peer_authenticated. PostgreSQL replication can be set to require TLS with CA-verified client certificates; the minimum TLS version and cipher list are tuned from the UI. The data/ sync runs over SSH.
  • Metrics store: listens on 127.0.0.1 only and is queried through the application. Its administrative endpoints (delete, snapshot, force-merge, reload, flags, profiling) require keys, generated by install-metrics-store.sh into the root-only /etc/satom/metrics-auth.env; the application holds only the snapshot key it needs.

The Monitoring dashboard's encryption card shows, per channel, whether it is encrypted, with which protocol and cipher, and how — each verdict backed by a live probe.

Read-only database access#

The Database tools SQL console, report widgets and plugin datasets run every query as the dedicated PostgreSQL role satom_console_ro, never as the application role. That role has no monitoring privileges and cannot read the credential tables or credential columns. When it is not provisioned the query is refused outright — there is no fallback to the application role. The installer creates it and every software update re-runs deploy/install-console-role.sh on the primary (the standby skips it and receives the role by replication). If the console reports the role as not usable, run sudo bash /opt/satom/deploy/install-console-role.sh on the primary and restart the application.

Outbound connections chosen by a user#

The certificate inspector and transaction tracer connect from the server to a destination. In inventory mode the target is a managed appliance or pool member. Free mode (any host:port) requires monitoring.probe_free and is audited; cloud instance-metadata addresses are always refused. Inventory mode allows a managed appliance only on its own port.

Network Architecture probes, monitor HTTPS probes and process http_check steps use the same guard and refuse loopback entirely. In every mode the node's own internal services (PostgreSQL 5432, the application on 8000, the metrics store on 8428) are refused. A name is resolved once and the connection goes to that address, so a DNS answer that changes between check and connect cannot redirect it. The DNS tool refuses names and servers that start with -.

Audit trail#

Successful sign-ins, 2FA sign-ins, every failed local sign-in (login.fail), lockouts, attempts against a locked account, directory sign-in failures (login.external_fail), idle session locks (session.idle_lock), configuration changes and administrative actions (including system backup, git bundle, firmware pull, code rollback, software update, deploy-automation mode, HA mode, promotion and HA node changes) are written to the audit log with the user and the real client IP (resolved the same way as for rate limiting). The CLI's admin reset-password and admin unlock write an audit row as user cli/root. See Audit log.

Advanced Upload size

MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH is MAX_UPLOAD_MB (default 600) megabytes, so a runaway upload is rejected with 413 instead of exhausting a worker. The vhost the installer writes and the static sample deploy/nginx-vhost.conf both set client_max_body_size 400M, enough for the largest update package; keep at least that if you base a hand-written proxy on the sample.
